newsitem.title: MEXICO: Fears of lower Mexican coffee crop spurs upswing.
newsitem.headline: Fears of lower Mexican coffee crop spurs upswing.

text.p: Worries for a lower and a later Mexican coffee crop are spurring brokers to offer higher prices for national beans as rains continue to lash crops in some critical states, traders and exporters said Wednesday.
"It is raining like hell in Veracruz," said a source from one Mexico trading house.
The rains are fuelling fears of crop delays, with cherries not being able to dry properly in the easterly state which last year was Mexico's top producer state.

Mexican coffee has moved from trading at a discount to a premium in the past week, with brokers clamouring for what is left in stocks from the 1995-1996 harvest, especially as the rains are likely to put back the just-starting 1996-1997 crop.

"The crop is being delayed," said the trader, adding that higher prices were also being offered because predictions were that crops were also late in Guatemala and Costa Rica, which could make Mexico and Central American beans scarce in the traditional early crop period of November and December.
Ernesto Gutierrez, the manager of Cafe de Chiapas, said the tight supplies had roasters fearing they will be left without coffee.
"The bad weather in Veracruz and Puebla states is causing brokers to worry on top of the supply problem," said Gutierrez from the Tuxtla Gutierrez-based exporting and trading house.
Veracruz and Puebla are on Mexico's eastern flank have traditionally been Mexico's second and third producer states.

But last harvest, Chiapas, normally the largest growing state, suffered its worst crop in decades and Veracruz jumped into the number one spot with a harvest around 1.7 million 60 kg bags, up from the 992,833 bags in 1994-1995.
Hurricanes and tropical storms have brought prolonged heavy rains to Veracruz and Puebla, probably causing some slight damage to beans, but almost certainly delaying harvesting, traders said.
Hurricane Josephine passed through the Gulf of Mexico this week, dumping a new round of rains on Veracruz, causing widespread flooding in lowland areas.

Also, Mexico's coffee harvest is seen down this year in its usual one-good-year, one-bad-year cycle. Last cycle was a bumper harvest so this one should be lower, even though the Chiapas harvest should recover, with reports of good flowerings and solid bean maturing.
Jenaro Hernandez de la Mora, executive director of the Association of Mexican Coffee Exporters, said he did not agree that the Veracruz crop would be too delayed.

A grower in Veracruz himself with a farm at 1,100 meters, Hernandez said the rains had brought a problem of very uneven flowerings. "We will have a long harvest with low volumes," he said of his home state.

He has already harvested a first small batch of beans and he predicted he would still be collecting beans in April, against the normal Veracruz harvest period of November to March, peaking at the end of January.

Hernandez said the price upswing also had much to do with U.S. brokers realising that Mexican might soon not be subject a four percent export tax in Europe so they are bidding up prices so as not to lose customers.

Mexico is putting pressure on the European Union to lift the tax and the export sector is quietly confident it could happen in the new year. "We will have a new market and U.S. brokers are acting before it happens," said Hernandez.
